title: Getting Around Bengaluru
subtitle: Autos, directions, and surviving the chaos
description: Survive the auto rickshaw negotiation, ask for directions in Bengaluru's chaos, and find your way back home.

items.english: Can I get an auto rickshaw here?
items.context: Literally 'will I get an auto?' — a quick way to check availability rather than standing around waving fruitlessly
items.scenario: Asking a passer-by or shopkeeper whether autos typically stop in this area

items.context: The most important phrase in this entire course — say this the moment you sit down. Without it, you'll be quoted whatever the driver feels like charging
items.scenario: Every single time you get into an auto rickshaw in Bengaluru. Every. Single. Time.

items.context: For when you're negotiating a fixed-price ride — ask this upfront and confirm before you get in
items.scenario: When an auto refuses the meter and you need to negotiate a flat fare, or asking a bike taxi price

items.context: Fill in the destination — ge marks direction in Kannada, hōgabēku means 'need to go'. Works with any neighbourhood, landmark, or metro station name
items.scenario: Telling an auto driver or asking anyone for directions — Koramangalage hōgabēku, Whitefieldge hōgabēku

items.context: Bengalureans measure distance in time ('20 minutes') not kilometers — the answer will tell you whether to walk, auto, or metro
items.scenario: Before deciding whether to walk to a place or take transport — especially useful in new neighbourhoods

items.english: How much time will it take?
items.context: Time is more useful than distance in Bengaluru traffic — 5 km can take 5 minutes or 50 minutes depending on the hour
items.scenario: Planning whether to leave now or later, or deciding if it's worth the auto fare versus waiting for a bus

items.context: Bala means right side — pair with landmarks since Bengaluru street names are rarely posted or known
items.scenario: Giving directions to an auto driver who's lost, or following spoken directions from a helpful local

items.context: Eḍa means left side — combine with right, straight, and stop here to guide any driver to your destination
items.scenario: Directing your auto driver through a lane your GPS doesn't know about

items.context: Nēra means straight or directly — use it between turns when giving step-by-step directions
items.scenario: Guiding a driver who missed the turn and needs to go straight before the next one

items.context: Illi means here, nilisi means stop — say it clearly and with enough warning so the driver can actually brake
items.scenario: Whenever you've reached your destination in an auto or cab — don't wait for the driver to guess

items.context: Dāri means path or way, tōrisi means show — a polite and humble way to ask for directions from a stranger
items.scenario: When you're completely lost and need a local to physically point you in the right direction

items.context: BMTC buses are the cheapest way around the city once you know the routes — elli means where
items.scenario: Asking for the nearest bus stop, especially useful when you've just arrived in an unfamiliar area
items.imageQuery: bus stand stop public transport india

items.context: The Namma Metro is your best friend for avoiding Bengaluru traffic — learn the Purple and Green line stations near you
items.scenario: When you're above ground and need to find the nearest Namma Metro entry point

items.context: Hattira means near or close — when someone says this, always ask eṣṭu dūra? because 'nearby' in Bengaluru can still be a 20-minute ride
items.scenario: When a local reassures you that your destination is close — prepare to verify

items.context: Tumba means very, dūra means far — if a local says this, believe them and plan accordingly. Take the metro if possible
items.scenario: When you're considering whether to walk somewhere and want a local's honest assessment
